summary: Icecho is an audio-first sonification of the Arctic sea ice record: 48 NSIDC September maps, 1979 to 2026, each played as a chord whose note count comes from how much ice is in the frame. It is built for blind and low-vision listeners first, then for classrooms, museums and anyone who cannot read a dashboard — the same 48-year record, through the ear. The measured chord never fades to one note: 1979 is six voices, 2026 is four, and 2012 — the record low — is three. Then a closing coda, labelled on screen as composition, not data, leaves one voice alone to decay.
details:
Icecho’s The Last Note turns the Arctic sea ice record into an interactive, audio-first story. It uses 48 September maps from the NSIDC Sea Ice Index, covering 1979–2026, alongside annual daily minimum extent data.

Each year becomes a chord. The measured ice extent determines how many voices are heard, while features extracted from the map influence the sound. The 1979 chord has six voices, the 2012 record low has three, and 2026 has four. A final, clearly labelled coda leaves one voice to decay; it is composition, not a claim that the ice fell to one-sixth of its original extent.

The experience is designed for blind and low-vision listeners as well as classrooms and museums. It includes keyboard controls, screen-reader text, reduced-motion support and a hands-free listening mode. It has not undergone a formal accessibility user study.

To try it, download the repository, open dist/TheLastNote.html in a browser and click Play the last note. It runs offline without installation.
